stem: When conducting a mental status examination, which of the following is an example of THOUGHT disorder?
answer: The correct answer is A. All of these can be noticed through examination of the patient's speech, but pressured speech is a sign of mania — i.e. of disordered thought, rather than a purely mechanical speech abnormality. Mutism, tachylalia, cluttering and dysarthria describe the output, not the thinking behind it.

stem: When evaluating a patient's thought form, which of the following is TRUE?

options.html: A patient with "goal-directed" thought likely has a thought disorder.
In "circumstantial" thought form, the patient will never answer your question.
If someone's thoughts are completely unconnected, this is an example of "flight of ideas".
If a patient's thought form is abnormal, they must be suffering from psychosis.
"Twenty-five dollars is a lot of money! Large faces and eyes" is an example of derailing/loose associations.

answer:
The correct answer is E. The thought-form vocabulary, with each distractor corrected:

  • Goal-directed thought is normal — so A is wrong
  • Circumstantial thought may wander or deviate but will eventually return to the point — so B's "never" is wrong
  • Flight of ideas consists of thoughts that are somewhat connected — so C is describing derailment
  • Abnormal thought form may be seen in mania as well as psychosis — so D's "must" is wrong
  • Derailing / loose associations consists of thoughts which are completely unconnected ✓

stem: You have written a prescription and have your hand on the doorknob when Beverly tells you that actually her mother is taking Paxil (paroxetine) and it "works great". She begs you to prescribe it for her instead, and promises that she will take it faithfully. Two weeks later, you receive a panicked voicemail from Beverly saying that the Paxil must not be working because she is now experiencing new symptoms, including insomnia, dizziness/vertigo, diarrhea, vomiting, and decreased concentration. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these new symptoms?

options.html: It has only been 2 weeks, so the medication has not had time to take effect yet
Beverly has missed doses of her medication and is experiencing withdrawal symptoms
Beverly is having an adverse reaction to the Paxil and should discontinue the medication immediately
Beverly's illness has suddenly become worse, and the dose you prescribed is not high enough to counteract the symptoms
The symptoms are not related to the medication

answer:
The correct answer is B. Common withdrawal effects of paroxetine: dizziness, anxiety, irritability, panic attacks, labile mood, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased concentration, and "brain zaps". When discontinuing paroxetine, a gradual taper is used.

The link to Q2 and Q57 is the whole point: Paxil has the shortest half-life of the SSRIs, so missing even a single dose can produce withdrawal — and Beverly is the patient who "often forgets to take medications on time" (Q57).

stem:
Please read the following case vignette: When you go to see Maria for your initial assessment, she is wearing a black cocktail dress and large silver earrings. She agrees quite happily to answer your questions, and tells you that she was picked up by the police because she was outside in the middle of December wearing only this dress. When you ask her if she feels that this was safe, she tells you that "my love will keep me warm". Upon further questioning, she reveals that she was walking to a hotel where she believes that George Clooney is waiting to spend a romantic evening with her. She describes herself as feeling extremely happy and energetic, but does not believe that there is anything unusual happening. She denies any suicidal or homicidal ideation.

Which of the following correctly identifies elements of the mental status exam that are described in this case?

options.html: Cooperation: does not believe that there is anything unusual happening
Insight: She describes herself as feeling extremely happy and energetic
Hallucinations: She believes that George Clooney is waiting to spend a romantic evening with her
Endings: She denies any suicidal or homicidal ideation.
Appearance: She describes herself as feeling extremely happy and energetic

answer:
The correct answer is D. The vignette annotated by MSE domain:

Detail from the caseMSE domain
wearing a black cocktail dress and large silver earringsAppearance
agrees quite happily to answer your questionsCooperation
outside in December wearing only this dressBehaviour
"my love will keep me warm"Insight
believes George Clooney is waiting for herThought content
feeling extremely happyMood
does not believe anything unusual is happeningInsight
denies any suicidal or homicidal ideationEnding ✓

Note that C is wrong on category, not content: the George Clooney belief is a delusion (thought content), not a hallucination — there is no false perception.

stem: Gina's current complaint is that she has been feeling extremely "down" for the past four weeks, and you believe that she is experiencing a major depressive episode. Which of the following would cause you to suspect that her depression is of the "melancholic" subtype as opposed to the "atypical" subtype?

options.html: She often wakes up at 2 am and cannot get back to sleep.
She feels like her body is "encased in concrete" and it is hard for her to move.
She is very sensitive to feelings of rejection.
She has been eating and sleeping much more than normal.
If something good happens, such as having lunch with a friend, her mood briefly improves.

answer:
The correct answer is A. The two subtypes side by side:

MelancholicAtypical
distinctly "black" quality of mood—
worsening in the morning / early morning awakening ← A—
anorexiahyperphagia ← D
—hypersomnia ← D
anhedoniareactivity of mood ← E
guiltrejection sensitivity ← C
—"leaden paralysis" ← B

Every distractor is an atypical feature. See major depressive disorder.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam

stem: Gina complains that she has felt quite "low" since she was a teenager, and you wonder if she may be suffering from dysthymia. Which of the following excludes the diagnosis of dysthymia?

options.html: The presence of a major depressive episode at any time.
A period of one month when symptoms were completely absent.
The presence of a hypomanic episode at any time.
Presence of symptoms for greater than five years.

answer:
The correct answer is D. A hypomanic episode in the context of subthreshold depression meets criteria for cyclothymia instead — a different diagnosis, so it excludes dysthymia.

Each distractor is compatible with dysthymia:

  • A — major depressive episodes may occur, just not during the first two years
  • B — symptoms may never be absent for longer than 2 months, so one month is fine
  • C — dysthymia does interfere with functioning
  • E — it may last for many years

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q54-Q55, Q86. Tests [[05 - Depressive Disorders]].
stem: Mark is a 33-year-old male who was recently laid off from his job at a local coal mine. Since then, he has had difficulty sleeping, with frequent nightmares about losing his home due to inability to pay his mortgage. He feels that life is no longer worth living and that he has no future. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Adjustment disorder occurs in response to an identifiable stressor that is "subthreshold" for PTSD and acute stress disorder — both of which require a threat of death, severe physical injury, or sexual violation. Job loss is such a subthreshold stressor.

The rest of the trauma spectrum:

  • Acute stress disorder — lasts less than a month
  • PTSD — more than a month
  • Complex PTSD — a disorder on the dissociative spectrum occurring in the context of prolonged interpersonal violence (domestic abuse, childhood sexual abuse)

stem: Ms. Adams is brought in to the hospital by her boyfriend who is really worried since she has been running a fever and her muscles seem very rigid. On admission she appears diaphoretic, tachycardic and to be in some confusion. On history Ms. Adams is a 35-year-old female employed by Ford for the last ten years. Her mother has diabetes and her father has high blood pressure and cholesterol. Her medications include a multivitamin, Alesse and Risperidone. Before this episode she had been feeling well. What is at the top of your differential diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The risperidone in her medication list is the clue. Red flags for NMS:

  • severe muscular rigidity ("lead pipe" rigidity)
  • hyperthermia (> 38 °C)
  • autonomic instability
  • changes in level of consciousness

Contrast with serotonin syndrome (Q59, Q93): serotonin syndrome is hyperreflexic with clonus and follows serotonergic agents; NMS is rigid and follows dopamine blockade.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q24, Q32, Q52, Q80, Q95-Q96. Tests [[09 - Bipolar Disorders]].
stem: Ms. Mackenzie is a 20-year-old woman brought into the ER by her parents. They say that their daughter has been acting erratically for the last 8 days. She has not been sleeping and when she speaks it is at a rapid pace and often difficult to follow her train of thought. She has been working for a year trying to save up to move out on her own but has recently started blowing through her savings on clothing and electronics. When asked if this has happened before they mention a brief period when she was 18 where she wasn't sleeping and had a lot of energy but it wasn't nearly this bad. In fact, before this happened, they were actually concerned she may be suffering from depression since she went through a period where she seemed very down and stopped spending time with friends or doing any activities. Based on your diagnosis, what is the most appropriate medication to give Ms. Mackenzie to help her?
answer:
The correct answer is C — carbamazepine. The 8-day episode of decreased sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas and impulsive spending is a manic episode, making this bipolar I disorder — so she needs a mood stabilizer, and carbamazepine is the only one on the list.

The other four are all actively wrong for mania: sertraline and bupropion are antidepressants that can precipitate or worsen mania (see Q96); Ritalin (methylphenidate) is a stimulant; zopiclone is a hypnotic that treats only the insomnia.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q24, Q32, Q52, Q80, Q95-Q96. Tests [[09 - Bipolar Disorders]].
stem: While you are conducting a complete psychiatric evaluation, John tells you that seven years ago, he had a period of time when he had more energy than he has ever had, he no longer needed to sleep, and he spent excessive amounts of money. Which of the following would MOST lead you to believe that John was experiencing a manic episode (rather than hypomanic)?

options.html: John's symptoms lasted for ten days.
John's friends and family noticed that he seemed "different" and encouraged him to see a doctor.
John's mood was irritable rather than grandiose.
John believed that people around him could hear his thoughts.
John met all seven of the DSM-IV-TR criteria (DIGFAST)

answer:
The correct answer is D. The presence of psychosis, hospitalization, or severe functional impairment is always diagnostic of a manic episode — and the belief that others can hear his thoughts (thought broadcasting) is psychosis.

Why the other discriminators fail: hypomanic episodes have the same criteria as manic episodes — the mood can be irritable in either (killing C), the same number of criteria must be met (killing E), and in both there is a noticeable change from baseline and functional impairment (killing B). The one criterion that does differ is duration: mania requires 7 days versus 4 for hypomania — but A's ten days already exceeds both thresholds, so it does not discriminate either. See mania and hypomania.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q24, Q32, Q52, Q80, Q95-Q96. Tests [[09 - Bipolar Disorders]].
stem: Edward is a 21-year-old male who presents to your office with complaints of constantly feeling "hyper". He states that he can't sit still and he feels that his mind is constantly racing. He has extreme difficulties paying attention in class and is failing one of his classes due to not having completed the required work. Which of the following would MOST suggest a diagnosis of ADHD as opposed to bipolar disorder?

options.html: Edward's first symptoms occurred around the age of 14.
Edward only sleeps for 2-3 hours per night, but wakes up refreshed.
Edward has never had a period of time during which he did not have these symptoms.
Edward has a family history of bipolar disorder.
Edward believes that he is an excellent student and does not need to study because of his genius intellect.

answer:
The correct answer is C. ADHD can be distinguished from mania in that it does not fluctuate, onsets in early childhood, and does not include insomnia, hypersexuality, psychosis, or true euphoria.

The non-fluctuating course is the strongest discriminator — bipolar disorder is episodic by definition. Note that A points toward bipolar, since 14 is not "early childhood"; B (decreased need for sleep) and E (grandiosity) are manic criteria; and D is a bipolar risk factor.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q24, Q32, Q52, Q80, Q95-Q96. Tests [[09 - Bipolar Disorders]].
stem: A 28-year-old female presents to the outpatient clinic with a history of recurrent episodes of both elevated and depressed mood, along with periods of mixed symptoms such as irritability, agitation, and sleep disturbances. During elevated episodes, she reports feeling excessively energetic, having racing thoughts, and engaging in impulsive behaviors. During depressive episodes, she feels sad, hopeless, and has thoughts of self-harm. You suspect bipolar type 1 disorder. Which of the following statements is true regarding the diagnosis of bipolar type 1 disorder?

options.html: Diagnosis requires the presence of at least one manic or mixed episode
Diagnosis requires the presence of at least one hypomanic episode
Diagnosis requires the presence of at least two manic or mixed episodes
Diagnosis requires the presence of at least two hypomanic episodes

answer:
The correct answer is A. Bipolar type 1 is diagnosed when a patient has experienced at least one manic or mixed episode.

  • A manic episode: elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsive or risky behaviours
  • A mixed episode: symptoms of both manic and depressive episodes
  • Hypomanic episodes are a milder form of mania and are typically associated with bipolar type 2

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q24, Q32, Q52, Q80, Q95-Q96. Tests [[09 - Bipolar Disorders]].
stem: What is the first-line treatment for bipolar type 1 disorder?

options.html: Mood stabilizers such as lithium or valproate

answer:
The correct answer is B. Mood stabilizers such as lithium and valproate are first-line for bipolar type 1, used to stabilize mood and prevent manic and depressive episodes.

  • SSRIs are not first line, as they can induce mania or hypomania — the same reason sertraline and bupropion were wrong in Q32
  • Benzodiazepines are for short-term relief of anxiety and insomnia
  • Antipsychotics may be used for acute manic or mixed episodes, but not typically as first-line maintenance therapy

stem: Which of the following is a common side effect of SSRIs?
answer:
The correct answer is E. The acronym is the drug class's own name — "SSRIs":

  • S — Sexual side effects
  • S — Sleep disturbance
  • R — Restlessness
  • I — Indigestion
  • S — Serotonin syndrome

See SSRIs and serotonin syndrome.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: Which SSRI medication is the best for avoiding SSRI withdrawal syndrome?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Fluoxetine (Prozac) has the longest half-life of the SSRIs and is therefore best for avoiding discontinuation syndrome. Paroxetine (Paxil) has the shortest half-life and is therefore the worst.

This single fact drives four questions in this section — Q2, Q51, Q57 and Q61. Learn the two extremes and the rest follow.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of Celexa (citalopram)?

options.html: Inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake by the post-synaptic neuron
Inhibition of serotonin reuptake by the post-synaptic neuron
Inhibition of serotonin reuptake by the pre-synaptic neuron
Inhibition of dopamine reuptake by the pre-synaptic neuron.

answer: The correct answer is C. Celexa is an SSRI, which inhibits reuptake by the pre-synaptic neuron, resulting in increased signalling to the post-synaptic neuron. Note that both the neurotransmitter and the neuron must be right — B has the correct transmitter but the wrong side of the synapse.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: Beverly is a 24-year-old woman followed by you for major depression. You have decided that the best treatment option for her is an SSRI. Beverly tells you that she often forgets to take medications on time. Which of the following would be the MOST appropriate SSRI to prescribe in this case?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Prozac has an extremely long half-life and is a good choice for patients who are inconsistent with dosing, as they will not go into withdrawal.

Paxil has the shortest half-life of the SSRIs and therefore prompts the worst withdrawal — it may produce symptoms after missing a single dose, which is exactly what happens in Q51.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: While taking Paxil (paroxetine), Beverly is admitted to the hospital with a kidney stone and she is given Demerol (meperidine) for pain relief. Shortly thereafter, the nursing staff notices that she is increasingly confused and agitated. Her heart rate and blood pressure are increased, and she has a fever. When you examine her, you note increased reflexes and clonus in her lower limbs. Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate next step?

options.html: Administer naloxone for suspected opiate overdose and discontinue Demerol.
Administer a short acting anti-hypertensive to lower her blood pressure.
Initiate external cooling and hydration measures to reduce core temperature.

answer:
The correct answer is A. The combination of meperidine and paroxetine has triggered serotonin syndrome, whose three symptom clusters are:

  • Autonomic hyperactivity — tachycardia, sweating, hyperthermia, mydriasis, flushing, shivering
  • Neuromuscular — clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertonia
  • Cognitive — confusion, agitation, hyperactivity

Management is discontinuation of all serotonergic agents plus supportive care for hyperthermia and hypertension, and there is some evidence that cyproheptadine (an anti-serotonergic agent) may help. So B, C, D and E are all reasonable.

Naloxone would not be appropriate because the patient is not experiencing an opiate overdose — the reflexes and clonus point the opposite way (opioid toxicity gives depressed reflexes and pinpoint pupils).

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: After trying Paxil for three months at increasing doses, Beverly's depression is no better. You decide to try augmenting the Paxil with an antidepressant from another class. Which of the following medications is absolutely contraindicated for this purpose?
answer: The correct answer is E. Caution must be exercised combining any two serotonergic agents — that is a relative contraindication. But the combination of MAOIs (Nardil/phenelzine, Parnate/tranylcypromine) with any other serotonergic agent is absolutely contraindicated.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: Beverly decides that she wants to stop taking her Paxil (paroxetine) entirely, but when you try to reduce her dose, she complains of intolerable withdrawals. You advise switching her to another SSRI before tapering. Which of the following SSRIs do you recommend?
answer: The correct answer is C. Prozac's long half-life makes it much less likely to cause severe withdrawals than Paxil, and it will be easier to taper. This is the fourth application of the half-life fact from Q2.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate step in the management of a TCA overdose?

options.html: Administer IV bicarbonate for severe acidosis
Consider decontamination with gastric lavage or activated charcoal if within one hour of ingestion.
Administer IV fluids and/or inotropes to correct hypotension
Order an ECG immediately to assess for conduction changes.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Antiarrhythmics should be avoided in TCA overdose, as they may increase the likelihood of developing ventricular tachycardia in the context of a long QT.

The rest are appropriate: decontamination may be considered within the first hour, and activated charcoal binds TCAs; TCA overdose causes QT changes so an ECG must be ordered; and IV bicarbonate and fluids/inotropes address the acidosis and hypotension.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of taking two different medications: sertraline for depression and tramadol for chronic pain. The patient reports feeling agitated, confused, and experiencing tremors and muscle stiffness. He also complains of sweating and a rapid heart rate. Which of the following conditions do you suspect?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The combination of sertraline — which inhibits serotonin reuptake — and tramadol — a pain medication that also affects serotonin reuptake — can produce an excess of serotonin, causing serotonin syndrome. Symptoms include agitation, confusion, tremors, muscle stiffness, sweating and rapid heart rate.

Contrast Q24: the same clinical picture following an antipsychotic would be NMS. The drug history is what separates them.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q56-Q57, Q59-Q62, Q93-Q94. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]], [[07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology]].
stem: For the patient in question 93, what is the treatment for his condition?

options.html: Discontinuation of the offending agents and supportive care

answer:
The correct answer is D. The first step is to discontinue the medications causing the serotonin excess — in some cases this alone is enough. Supportive care includes hydration, monitoring vital signs, and medications to control agitation and muscle stiffness.

C is the near-miss: in severe cases, serotonin receptor blockers such as cyproheptadine may be used — but that is not the first-line answer. Benzodiazepines and antipsychotics are not typically used and may worsen the condition (though benzodiazepines can be used for sedation).

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q65. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]].
stem: Which of the following patient factors DECREASES the likelihood that electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) will be successful in MDD?
answer: The correct answer is E — chronic pain. Older age, anorexia, catatonia and psychomotor retardation are all positive predictors of ECT response in MDD; comorbid chronic pain predicts a poorer response.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q65. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]].
stem: Which of the following is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)?

options.html: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT.

answer: The correct answer is E. All of the above are relative contraindications, but no absolute contraindications to ECT exist. ECT is a safe and effective management option for depression — a point the workbook makes again in Q77 for the elderly.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q65. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]].
stem: Which of the following would be appropriate counselling for a patient regarding starting an MAOI?

options.html: Patients should avoid eating aged cheeses or preserved foods as this may precipitate serotonin syndrome.
Concurrent use of Imitrex (sumatriptan) may precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
Patients can switch between antidepressants by gradually decreasing the dose of their SSRI antidepressant while simultaneously increasing their dose of an MAOI.
The mechanism of the interaction between MAOIs and aged/pickled/smoked foods involves tyramine metabolism.
MAOIs are an appropriate first line treatment for children and adolescents with severe depression.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Aged cheeses and pickled/smoked foods contain tyramine, which cannot be metabolized in the presence of MAOIs and leads to a hypertensive crisis by increasing NE activity.

A and B are the same two facts with their consequences swapped: the food interaction causes a hypertensive crisis (not serotonin syndrome, killing A), while sumatriptan is serotonergic and could precipitate serotonin syndrome (not a hypertensive crisis, killing B).

C is dangerous: MAOIs must not be given concurrently with any other serotonergic antidepressant — there must be a "wash out" period, recommended 2 weeks. E is wrong because although effective, MAOIs are not first line for depression/anxiety and are not usually given to children because of their side effect profile.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q25. Tests [[08 - Suicide]].
stem: Ms. Edwards is a 35-year-old woman who was admitted to the hospital after her most recent suicide attempt. Her husband came home early from his camping trip and found her unconscious in the garage with the car turned on. This is not Ms. Edwards' first time attempting suicide. 2 years ago she took a bunch of pills but her husband found the empty bottles and she was rushed to the hospital and treated. When speaking with her about what happened she mentions that she wished her husband hadn't found her and that she would consider trying again. When prompted she mentions different ways of committing suicide but doesn't seem to have settled on anything or have a concrete plan. What factor makes her most at risk for committing suicide over the next 5 years?

options.html: The fact that her method of previous attempts had a high lethality
The fact that this is her second time attempting suicide
The fact that she has a vague idea of how she would attempt suicide again
The fact that she is female
The fact that she is over 30

answer:
The correct answer is A. When previous attempts have had high lethality, individuals are more likely to have completed suicide at 5-year follow-up. Carbon monoxide poisoning in a closed garage is a high-lethality method.

The other options are all genuine considerations that are simply weaker predictors than lethality of method — and note D is the wrong direction: female sex is associated with more attempts but lower completion.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Anais is a ten-year-old girl who you have diagnosed with clinical depression. Her mother also has clinical depression and tells you that she is confused by your diagnosis, since Anais' mood does not at all resemble what the mother experiences when she is depressed. Which of the following is TRUE regarding the differences between depression in children and in adults?

options.html: Anais would be less likely to experience irritability and anxiety than an adult.
Pretend play that centers on death and dying is the equivalent of Anais' mother saying that she wants to commit suicide.
It would not be concerning if Anais were to maintain her present weight for an extended period of time.
If Anais were to hear voices or see things, this would automatically be a sign of a severe depression.
If Anais had had subthreshold symptoms of depression for a year, this would not meet criteria for dysthymia.

answer:
The correct answer is B. Four developmental differences, each correcting one option:

  • Children tend to experience greater irritability (and anxiety) — kills A
  • They may fail to reach expected weight gains rather than losing weight — so a child holding a static weight is concerning, killing C
  • They may report psychotic-like experiences even in the context of mild depression — so hallucinations are not automatically a marker of severity, killing D
  • Dysthymia may be diagnosed after 1 year in children (versus 2 years in adults) — killing E
  • Children may express suicidal ideation as death-related play ✓

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Anais' mother asks you what treatment is the most likely to help Anais feel better. What do you tell her?

options.html: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) is a safe and effective treatment for young children with depression.
The only first line pharmacological treatment for depression in children is Cipralex (escitalopram).
Combining cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) with an SSRI does not provide any additional benefit in children with severe depressive symptoms.
If Anais' depression is treated with cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), her mother can expect her therapy to last for 1-2 years.
If Anais is started on an SSRI, she would be given an adult dose.

answer:
The correct answer is E. SSRIs are not dosed by age or weight — a child receives an adult dose.

The rest of the treatment picture:

  • Options for children are SSRI medication and CBT. IPT may be used in adolescents, but not in children — kills A
  • The only first-line SSRI is fluoxetine (Prozac) — all others are second line, killing B
  • The optimal treatment for severe depression is CBT combined with medication — killing C
  • CBT is a short-term therapy which can last as little as 6-12 weeks, with possible "booster" sessions afterwards — killing D

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Janice goes to see a therapist because of her severe social anxiety and obsessive compulsive disorder. Which of the following is MOST LIKELY to be true?

options.html: A cognitive therapist would ask Janice to write down the thoughts that she has about how people are evaluating her in social situations, and attempt to challenge those thoughts.
A therapist practicing ERP (a subtype of CBT) would ask Janice to approach a situation that she fears without engaging in a ritual for a maximum of five minutes.
A behavioural therapist would focus on how Janice's actions reflect experiences from her past.
A psychodynamic psychiatrist would not be interested in details of Janice's childhood and developmental history.
A therapist practicing IPT would not explicitly process Janice's feelings about termination, as IPT does not usually work with transference.

answer:
The correct answer is A. The modality map:

  • A cognitive therapist focuses on modifying problematic cognitions that impair function ✓
  • A behavioural therapist focuses on modifying behaviour in the present — so C (past experiences) is describing psychodynamic work
  • In Exposure and Response Prevention, the patient remains in the situation until her anxiety subsides, without performing any rituals — so B's "maximum of five minutes" is wrong; the endpoint is habituation, not the clock (compare Q4's "Prolonged")
  • A psychodynamic psychiatrist would focus on the impact of childhood experiences and conflicts — killing D

flags.title: Name inconsistency
flags.html: The stem introduces "Janice" but the options and the key alternate between Janice and Janet (and Q73-74's key refers to Janet). Same patient.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a potential area of focus for IPT?
answer: The correct answer is E — social isolation. The four IPT focus areas are grief, role transition, interpersonal conflict and interpersonal deficit. Social isolation is a consequence that IPT may address, not one of its named problem areas.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter and the phrase only.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is similar across therapeutic modalities as practiced in the community?

options.html: Strict adherence to a single approach

answer:
The correct answer is A. Resistance is normal and expected in all types of therapy, and is not always under the patient's conscious control.

Therapies vary in their use of transference, adherence to goal setting, and frequency of meetings — killing B, C and D. And E is the opposite of practice: while community therapists may have an area of focus, it is most common to practice an eclectic-integrative approach focused on the needs of the client.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q78-Q79. Tests [[11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses]].
stem: Common comorbidities that occur with chronic pain include all but?
answer:
The correct answer is E. The real comorbidity rates in chronic pain:

  • Depression occurs in 8-50%
  • Anxiety as a symptom occurs in 50%; an anxiety disorder in 19-30%
  • Substance misuse — higher than the general population
  • Anger — many report it

Psychosis is not on the list.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q78-Q79. Tests [[11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses]].
stem: Brenda is a 19-year-old woman who is currently undergoing treatment for breast cancer, and presents to you with concerns about her mood. Her appetite is decreased, she has no desire to see her friends, and she cries for most of the day. She does not sleep well and complains of initial insomnia as well as frequent awakenings. You wonder if you should prescribe an SSRI to help with her symptoms. Which of the following is TRUE about management of Brenda's condition?

options.html: The majority of patients with a medical illness will meet criteria for major depression at some point during their illness.
You will need to rule out adjustment disorder, since supportive psychotherapy would be superior to an SSRI for that diagnosis.
Because of Brenda's medical condition, SSRI medications should be given at a lower dose than a healthy adult would receive.
Paxil (paroxetine) would be the best choice of SSRI for a woman receiving tamoxifen.
If Brenda is treated with an SSRI, psychotherapy will likely not be necessary.

answer:
The correct answer is B. If the diagnosis were adjustment disorder, supportive psychotherapy would be superior to an SSRI — so it must be ruled out first.

Each distractor:

  • A — fewer than 30% of patients with a medical illness meet criteria for depression
  • C — SSRIs should still be given at the normal dose
  • D — Paxil decreases blood levels of tamoxifen and would be a poor choice in a breast cancer patient
  • E — psychotherapy may be useful as an adjunct

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q78-Q79. Tests [[11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses]].
stem: You initiate therapy with Cipralex (escitalopram), and Brenda's symptoms improve. You continue to follow her over the course of treatment for her cancer. Which of the following is TRUE about Brenda's experience?

options.html: The successful treatment of her depression has the potential to improve her prognosis.
As Brenda's treatment nears an end, you can expect her to experience a sense of relief and improvement in her mood.
Her age and gender put her in a lower risk bracket for developing depression as a result of medical illness.
Brenda's desire to conquer her illness will likely prevent her from considering suicide.
Brenda's depression is likely psychological and does not have a physiological basis.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Successful treatment of depression has the potential to improve the prognosis of the medical illness itself.

B is the counterintuitive point worth keeping: high-risk times for depression include at the point of diagnosis and at the completion of treatment, as social support may decrease and patients must emerge from "survival mode" and begin to reorganize their lives. So the end of treatment is a risk period, not a relief.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q58. Tests [[12 - Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages]].
stem: Beverly tells you that she is considering becoming pregnant, and wants to know if there is an SSRI that pregnant women can take safely. Of the SSRIs, you tell her that __________ carries a risk of serious birth defects, and that __________ is considered to be comparatively safe.
answer: The correct answer is A. Paxil (paroxetine) carries a risk of serious birth defects; Prozac (fluoxetine) is considered comparatively safe.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. Note that paroxetine is the problem drug in three consecutive questions — worst withdrawal (Q51, Q57), teratogenicity (Q58) — which is a reasonable way to remember it.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: A person with Social anxiety disorder (SAD) will finish this statement: When I am in a crowd of people, I worry that…

options.html: I will get contaminated with everyone's germs
I will do something embarrassing and everyone will look at me and laugh
I will feel closed in and panicky
I will run into a clown

answer:
The correct answer is B. People with SAD worry about being judged and about embarrassing themselves, especially in social situations.

The distractors are the same crowd from four other diagnoses' points of view: A is OCD (contamination), C is paranoia, D is panic disorder/agoraphobia, E is a specific phobia.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Blood/injection/injury type phobias differ from other phobia subtypes in that:

options.html: They cause a decrease in blood pressure
Applied muscle tension does not work

answer:
The correct answer is A. Blood/injection/injury phobias cause a decrease in blood pressure — a vasovagal response — whereas other phobias produce sympathetic arousal with a rise in BP.

That physiology is also why applied muscle tension is the specific treatment for this subtype (making D false).
